title: Scoring systems for the prediction of choledocholithiasis: systematic review and meta-analysis (protocol)

2 1. Background 21 Choledocholithiasis is a major cause of hospitalization and the leading cause of symptomatic 22 cholelithiasis and acute biliary pancreatitis [1]. Cholelithiasis and cholecystitis afflicts more than 20 23 million Americans annually at an estimated cost of $16.3 billion, resulting in 350,000 24 hospitalizations and 15,000 deaths [2]. The prevalence of choledocholithiasis is approximately 10% 25 to 15% in patients with symptomatic cholelithiasis [3]. Up to one-third of patients with 26 choledocholithiasis spontaneously excrete stones without intervention, but the majority of patients 27 require endoscopic and/or surgical intervention [4]. Therefore, choledocholithiasis should be 28 detected and managed as soon as possible [5]. 29 The diagnosis of choledocholithiasis is challenging because the initial investigations 30 including medical history, physical examination, laboratory tests, and transabdominal ultrasound 31 (TUS) have low diagnostic accuracy [6, 7]. The next options of diagnostic examination for 32 cholelithiasis is imaging such as magnetic resonance cholangiography (MRCP), endoscopic 33 retrograde cholangiography (ERCP), endoscopic ultrasound (EUS), intraoperative cholangiography 34 (IOC) [8]. MRCP is a non-invasive and accurate test compared to ERCP, but the main disadvantage 35 of MRCP is that the identified common bile duct stones need to be removed by another intervention 36 method [9]. EUS shows excellent diagnostic accuracy equivalent to MRCP, and EUS followed by 37 ERCP is a cost-effective method because both EUS and ERCP can be performed in the same session 38 [10]. However, ERCP is associated with adverse events in 6% to 15%, some life-threatening [11]. 39 IOC is a gold standard technique for the diagnosis of intraoperative choledocholithiasis, but its 40 disadvantages include radiation exposure, some failure rates, and increased surgery time [12]. 41 Scoring systems for predicting choledocholithiasis has been attracting attention because the 42 risk of choledocholithiasis can be evaluated, the next necessary tests and treatments can be decided, 43 and unnecessary tests can be avoided. The American Society of Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASGE) 44 published the algorithm that may be helpful for managing patients with suspected choledocholithiasis 45

3 dependent on their risk stratification [13]. Some studies evaluating external validity have shown that 46 the ASGE’s algorithm has poor diagnostic accuracy [14–20]. After publication of the ASGE’s 47 algorithm, in the last years, at least four new scoring systems for the prediction of 48 choledocholithiasis were published [21–24]. 49 The present study will aim to assess the scoring systems for predicting choledocholithiasis. 50 51 2. Objectives 52 We will summarize the reported multivariable scoring systems for predicting choledocholithiasis 53 (PART A), and assess the predictive performance of scoring systems for choledocholithiasis (PART 54 B). 55 56 3. Methods 57 3.1. Protocol 58 To qualify the study, we will follow the prognostic model study definition proposed in the Critical 59 Appraisal and Data Extraction for Systematic Reviews (CHARMS) [25]. We will publish this 60 protocol in protocols.io (https://www.protocols.io/). 61 3.2 Criteria for considering studies for this review 62 3.2.1 Types of studies 63 We will include all studies on the development, the update, and/or the external validation of at least 64 one multivariable model or scoring system for predicting choledocholithiasis. A multivariable model 65 will be a mathematical equation that relates multiple predictors for participants with suspected 66 choledocholithiasis to the probability of choledocholithiasis. 67 We will include studies reported as full text, those published as abstract only, and unpublished data. 68 There is no restriction regarding publication language. 69 3.2.2 Types of participants 70

4 We will include studies in adults aged >18 years with suspected choledocholithiasis in any setting. 71 We will exclude studies that look for risk factors for choledocholithiasis but have no score. 72 73 3.3 Outcomes 74 3.3.1 Primary outcomes 75 We will assess the quality of studies which develop or validate scoring systems for the prediction of 76 choledocholithiasis. 77 We will assess the predictive performance of scoring systems for choledocholithiasis in model 78 validation studies. 79 80 3.3.2 Secondary outcomes 81 We will review and appraise the validity and usefulness of the scoring systems for the prediction of 82 choledocholithiasis. 83 We will assess reported performance of scoring systems for the prediction of choledocholithiasis. 84 85 3.4 Search methods for identification of studies 86 3.4.1 Electronic searches 87 We will search the following electronic databases: 88 1. Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL); and 89 2. EMBASE (1988 to present). 90 We will also search the following clinical trial registers/trial result registers: 91 1. Clinical Trials.gov; and 92 2. the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Platform Search Portal (ICTRP). 93

5 We will check the reference lists of included studies and review articles for additional references. We 94 will search the reference lists of guidelines for related to choledocholithiasis [13]. We will contact 95 authors of identified trials and ask them to obtain additional data. 96 97 3.5 Data collection and analysis 98 3.5.1 Selection of studies 99 Two review authors (JW and TS) will independently screen titles and abstracts for inclusion. All of 100 the potential studies we identify as a result of the search will be coded them as either ‘retrieve’ 101 (eligible, potentially eligible, or unclear) or ‘do not retrieve’. We will retrieve the full text of 102 potentially eligible studies and two review authors (JW and TS) will independently screen the full 103 text, and identify studies for inclusion, and identify and record reasons for exclusion of the ineligible 104 studies. We will resolve any disagreement through discussion or, if required, we will consult a third 105 author (TK and/or YK). We will identify and exclude duplicates and collate multiple reports of the 106 same study, so that each study rather than each report is the unit of interest in the review. We will 107 record the selection process in sufficient detail to complete a PRISMA flow diagram and 108 'Characteristics of excluded studies' table. 109 110 3.5.2 Data extraction and management 111 We will use a standardized data collection form for study characteristics and outcome data, which 112 will be piloted on at least one study included in the review. Two review authors (JW and TS) will 113 independently extract study characteristics from included studies. 114 We will extract the following data in accordance with the Critical Appraisal and Data Extraction for 115 Systematic Reviews (CHARMS) [25]:source of data or study design (development and validation) 116 (eg, prospective, case control, cohort, clinical consensus), study characteristics (development and 117 validation) (eg, country, year, number of centers), participant characteristics (development and 118

6 validation) (eg, number, age, sex, setting), predicted outcome (development and validation) (eg, 119 choledocholithiasis diagnosis confirmed), model development (development) (eg, sample size, type 120 of model (eg, logistic, neural network, machine learning techniques), handling of continuous 121 variables (eg, complete-case analysis, imputation, or other methods), selection of variables, missing 122 data, method of internal validation), model presentation (development) (eg, full regression model, 123 simplified model, score chart), assessment of performance (development and validation) (eg, 124 measures of discrimination (eg, c-statistic), measures of calibration (eg, expected/observed events), 125 classification measures (eg, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive 126 value)). 127 128 3.6 Assessment of risk of bias in included studies 129 Two review authors (JW and TS) will independently assess the risk of bias for each study included in 130 the review, using the Prediction model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (PROBAST) [26]. We will 131 resolve any disagreement by discussion, or by involving a third review author (TK and/or YK). We 132 will assess the risk of bias according to 23 signalling questions within four domains (participant 133 selection, predictors, outcome and analysis). The models will be classed as low, high or unclear risk 134 of bias. 135 136 3.7 Data synthesis 137 We will summarize the results using descriptive statistics and a narrative synthesis. We will not 138 perform a quantitative synthesis of the scores or their predictive performance in model development 139 studies. However, if we identify multiple studies that evaluate the same scoring system and report 140 common performance measures in model validation studies, we will perform a random effects meta-141 analysis to calculate a summary estimate for models’ performance and calibration. We will also 142 consider for the meta-analysis those prediction models that will be internally validated through 143

7 bootstrapping or cross validation and will be externally validated in only two independent datasets. 144 We will follow a recently published framework for the meta-analysis of prediction models. If a 145 measure of uncertainty (standard error or 95% confidence interval) is not available for mean C 146 statistic, we will use a formula to approximate the standard error of mean C statistic based on number 147 of events and number of participants. We will quantify between study heterogeneity by using the I2 148 and τ2 statistics. 149 We will perform the meta-analysis using RevMan 5.4.1 (The Cochrane Collaboration, Copenhagen, 150 Denmark), Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-Analysis software, version 1.25 [27], or STATA 151 software, version 16.0 (Stata Corporation, College Station, TX). 152 153 3.8 Assessment of heterogeneity 154 If we perform meta-analyses in model validation studies, to investigate the potential sources of 155 heterogeneity, we will assess the effects of the following factors on the predictive performance of 156 scoring systems for choledocholithiasis: setting (emergency department or patients admitted to 157 hospital). 158 159 3.9 Sensitivity analysis 160 If we perform meta-analyses in model validation studies, we will present sensitivity analyses 161 stratified by methodological quality as per the PROBAST. We will also perform the following 162 sensitivity analyses to investigate the robustness of the results: excluding studies that their reference 163 test is unknown. 164 165
